\chapter{The Meeting Comes Off the Page}
\label{ch:ur-script-meeting}
\hlchaptermodality{18}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can read aam, aasmaan, purana, aap, voh and hun off the page, name a non-joining letter on sight, and write the opening meeting exchange from dictation.}

The exchange the book opens with -- salam, aap ka naam kya hai, mera naam ... hai, aap kaise hain, main ... hun -- is readable and writable end to end for the first time, on letters taught across chapters one to eight.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ām]{\ur{آم} — \textquotedblleft{}mango,\textquotedblright{} and the name that did not travel}

\label{lesson:UR-C18-aam}



\begin{quote}
Write \ur{یہ} \ur{کام} \ur{ہے۔} and say it. Ten letters are yours.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{آم}} — \emph{ām} — \textbf{mango}
\end{quote}

Two letters. The second is \textbf{\ur{م}}, which you have written many times. The first looks like the tall stroke you know with a small wave lying across its head, and that wave is doing a real job — it is the next lesson's whole subject.

\textbf{\ur{آم}} is masculine.

\begin{quote}
\emph{yih ām hai.} — \textquotedblleft{}This is a mango.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Say that now; you can already write every word in it except the first letter of \textbf{\ur{آم}}, and that letter arrives shortly.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{آم}} is \textbf{inherited}: Sanskrit \emph{āmra} became Prakrit \emph{amba} and then Urdu \emph{ām}, the ordinary north Indian name for the fruit for as long as there has been a north Indian name for it.

Now the part worth slowing down for. English calls the fruit \textbf{mango}, and a reader who has newly learned \emph{ām} would reasonably guess the two words are relatives. They are not.

\textbf{mango} came by sea. Portuguese traders on the Malabar coast met the fruit under its \textbf{Dravidian} name — Tamil and Malayalam \emph{māṅkāy}, \textquotedblleft{}mango fruit\textquotedblright{} — carried it home as \emph{manga}, and English took it from Portuguese. So the fruit travelled to Europe wearing a southern Indian name while the northern name stayed where it was.

Two unrelated words for one fruit inside one country, and the one that left is not the one you are learning. That is worth holding: a resemblance is evidence of nothing on its own, and here there is not even a resemblance — the relationship people assume is the one that does not exist.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{ām} — mango; then \emph{yih ām hai}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the food and drink words so far — \textbf{ām, pānī, chāy, dūdh, roṭī}
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \textbf{ām} $\leftarrow$ Prakrit \emph{amba} $\leftarrow$ Sanskrit \emph{āmra}
  \item \emph{Trace it:} English \textbf{mango} $\leftarrow$ Portuguese \emph{manga} $\leftarrow$ Tamil and Malayalam \emph{māṅkāy} — a different road, from a different family
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ṭopī}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}this is a mango.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{yih ām hai.}) Which Indian language family gave English its word for the fruit? (\textbf{Dravidian} — Tamil and Malayalam.) Which one gave Urdu \textbf{\ur{آم}}? (\textbf{Indo-Aryan}, through Sanskrit.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D8\%A2\%D9\%85}{Wiktionary: \ur{آم}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[āsmān]{\ur{آسمان} — \textquotedblleft{}sky,\textquotedblright{} which used to mean stone}

\label{lesson:UR-C18-aasmaan}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}this is a mango.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{yih ām hai.}) Which family gave English its word for that fruit? (\textbf{Dravidian}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{آسمان}} — \emph{āsmān} — \textbf{sky}
\end{quote}

Six letters, and five of them are already yours: \textbf{\ur{س}}, \textbf{\ur{م}}, \textbf{\ur{ا}}, \textbf{\ur{ن}} — and the tall stroke that opens it, wearing the same small wave you met on \textbf{\ur{آم}}. One shape stands between you and reading this word off the page.

\textbf{\ur{آسمان}} is masculine.

\begin{quote}
\emph{āsmān nīlā hai.} — \textquotedblleft{}The sky is blue.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

That sentence reuses a colour you already own and the copula you learned to write back in chapter six.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{آسمان}} is \textbf{borrowed}, from Persian \emph{āsmān} — the same road that brought \emph{khudā}. Inside Iranian it is inherited, running back through Avestan \emph{asman-} to Proto-Indo-Iranian \emph{*aćman-} and to Proto-Indo-European \textbf{*h\textsubscript{2}é\'{k}mōn}.

And \textbf{*h\textsubscript{2}é\'{k}mōn} did not mean sky. It meant \textbf{stone}.

Follow it sideways and the family is unmistakable: Sanskrit \emph{aśman} \textquotedblleft{}stone,\textquotedblright{} Greek \emph{ákmōn} \textquotedblleft{}anvil,\textquotedblright{} Lithuanian \emph{akmuo} \textquotedblleft{}stone.\textquotedblright{} Through Germanic the standard reconstruction carries the same root into English as \textbf{hammer} — a word that named a stone tool long before anyone made one out of metal. That last step is the mainstream account rather than a settled one; specialists note formal difficulties with it, so hold it as probable rather than proven.

So how does stone become sky? Because the sky was pictured as a \textbf{vault of stone} arching overhead, and the word for the material became the word for the thing built of it. When you say \emph{āsmān}, you are calling the sky a stone in a language that stopped noticing centuries ago.

Set that beside \textbf{\ur{آم}} from the lesson before. There, a resemblance people expect turns out to be nothing. Here, a resemblance nobody would expect — \emph{āsmān} and \emph{hammer} — is probably real, on evidence rather than on sound. Neither one can be settled by how the words sound. Only the trail settles it, and sometimes the trail answers \textquotedblleft{}probably\textquotedblright{} rather than \textquotedblleft{}yes\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{āsmān} — sky; then \emph{āsmān nīlā hai}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the weather words so far — \textbf{āsmān, bārish, dhūp, hawā, garmī, sardī}
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \textbf{āsmān} $\leftarrow$ Persian $\leftarrow$ Avestan \emph{asman-} $\leftarrow$ PIE \emph{*h\textsubscript{2}é\'{k}mōn} \textquotedblleft{}stone\textquotedblright{} $\to$ English \textbf{hammer}
  \item \emph{Say it:} which of \textbf{\ur{آم}} and \textbf{\ur{آسمان}} has a real English cousin, and which has one people wrongly assume
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}the sky is blue.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{āsmān nīlā hai.}) Was \textbf{\ur{آسمان}} inherited or borrowed into Urdu? (\textbf{Borrowed}, from Persian.) Name its English cousin. (\textbf{Hammer}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D8\%A2\%D8\%B3\%D9\%85\%D8\%A7\%D9\%86}{Wiktionary: \ur{آسمان}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[purānā]{\ur{پرانا} — \textquotedblleft{}old,\textquotedblright{} and the word behind the Purāṇas}

\label{lesson:UR-C18-purana}



\begin{quote}
Write \ur{آسمان}. Two alifs, one wearing the wave and one not — say which is which as you draw them.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{پرانا}} — \emph{purānā} — \textbf{old}
\end{quote}

Five letters, and four are yours already: \textbf{\ur{ر}}, \textbf{\ur{ا}}, \textbf{\ur{ن}}, \textbf{\ur{ا}}. The one that opens it is new to your hand, and it is the next lesson.

\textbf{\ur{پرانا}} changes its ending to agree with the noun it describes, the way \textbf{\ur{کالا}} \emph{kālā} and \textbf{\ur{نیلا}} \emph{nīlā} do:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ur{پرانا}} \emph{purānā} with a masculine noun
  \item \textbf{\ur{پرانی}} \emph{purānī} with a feminine one
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\emph{yih kām purānā hai.} — \textquotedblleft{}This work is old.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{merī qamīz purānī hai.} — \textquotedblleft{}My shirt is old.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Say each, and notice you are choosing the ending by the noun's gender without being told which to use — you have made that choice for two chapters of colours already.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{پرانا}} is \textbf{inherited}: Sanskrit \emph{purāṇa}, \textquotedblleft{}ancient, belonging to former times,\textquotedblright{} built on \emph{purā}, \textquotedblleft{}formerly.\textquotedblright{} Behind that stands Proto-Indo-European \textbf{*per-}, in the sense \textquotedblleft{}forward, before.\textquotedblright{}

That root went everywhere. Greek \emph{pró}, Latin \emph{pro} and \emph{prior}, and in English a whole quiet family: \textbf{fore}, \textbf{former}, \textbf{first}, \textbf{before}. Each of them is a way of saying \textquotedblleft{}in front\textquotedblright{} that turned into a way of saying \textquotedblleft{}earlier\textquotedblright{} — and \textbf{\ur{پرانا}} made the same turn, in the same direction, in a different branch.

One more thing this word names. The Sanskrit texts called the \textbf{Purāṇas} are this very word, plural: literally \textquotedblleft{}the old ones,\textquotedblright{} a body of writing whose title is an adjective. When you say \emph{purānā} you are using the everyday form of a word that also names a library.

Beside \textbf{\ur{آم}}, this is the other kind of result. There, a link people expect turns out not to exist. Here, a link nobody expects — \emph{purānā} and English \emph{first} — turns out to hold, all the way down.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{purānā}, then \textbf{purānī}, and say what decides the ending
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{yih kām purānā hai}, then \emph{merī qamīz purānī hai}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the agreeing words you now have — \textbf{kālā, nīlā, purānā}
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \textbf{purānā} $\leftarrow$ Sanskrit \emph{purāṇa} $\leftarrow$ \emph{purā} $\leftarrow$ PIE \emph{*per-} $\to$ English \textbf{fore, former, first, before}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}this work is old.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{yih kām purānā hai.}) What does the name of the Purāṇas mean? (\textbf{The old ones}.) Name two English cousins of \textbf{\ur{پرانا}}. (\textbf{Fore, former, first, before} — any two.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D9\%BE\%D8\%B1\%D8\%A7\%D9\%86\%D8\%A7}{Wiktionary: \ur{پرانا}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ām, āsmān, ānā]{Eleven letters, and two kinds of answer}

\label{lesson:UR-C18-review-madda}



\begin{quote}
Write \ur{ا}, then \ur{آ}. Say what the wave does and where in a word it belongs. (\textbf{Long ā}; at the \textbf{start}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
Read from the right, naming letters before saying each word:

\begin{quote}
\ur{آم}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\ur{آسمان}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\ur{آنا}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\ur{ماں}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\ur{نہیں}
\end{quote}

And two sentences, whole:

\begin{quote}
\ur{آسمان} \ur{نیلا} \ur{ہے۔}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\ur{یہ} \ur{آم} \ur{ہے۔}
\end{quote}

\emph{āsmān nīlā hai.} — \emph{yih ām hai.}

Count what that took. Ten letters carried you to \emph{hai}; one more carried you to the sky.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Cover the page. Look, hide, write, uncover, repair.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ur{آم} — look, cover, write, uncover, repair
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ur{آسمان} — look, cover, write, uncover, repair
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ur{آسمان} \ur{نیلا} \ur{ہے۔} — the whole sentence, then compare
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{purānā}, and name the one letter in it your hand cannot yet make
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn — by ear}
Page shut. Three words, three etymologies, and two different verdicts — say which is which out loud.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{ām} and English \emph{mango} — related, or only assumed to be?
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{āsmān} and English \emph{hammer} — related, or only assumed to be?
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{purānā} and English \emph{first} — related, or only assumed to be?
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{yih ām purānā hai}, then \emph{merī qamīz purānī hai}
  \item \emph{Listen:} for the long ā opening \emph{ām}, \emph{āsmān} and \emph{ānā}, and hold it
\end{itemize}

The point of putting those three together is that \textbf{the sound tells you nothing}. \emph{ām} and \emph{mango} look like a match and are not one. \emph{āsmān} and \emph{hammer} look like nothing at all and are probably cousins. Only the trail decides, and it is allowed to answer \textquotedblleft{}probably\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many letters can you write? (\textbf{Eleven}.) Write \textquotedblleft{}the sky is blue.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{\ur{آسمان} \ur{نیلا} \ur{ہے۔}}) Which word in this lesson is still waiting on a letter? (\emph{\textbf{purānā}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[voh]{\ur{وہ} — \textquotedblleft{}that,\textquotedblright{} and everyone who is not here}

\label{lesson:UR-C18-voh}



\begin{quote}
Write \ur{آپ}. Say where pe's three dots sit, and who you would address as \emph{āp}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{وہ}} — \emph{voh} — \textbf{that}; and \textbf{he}, \textbf{she}, \textbf{they}
\end{quote}

Two letters. The second is \textbf{\ur{ہ}}, closing the word with its round curl. The first is \textbf{\ur{و}}, which you learned to write in chapter eight.

\textbf{\ur{وہ}} is the far partner of \textbf{\ur{یہ}}. One points at what is beside you; the other points at what is over there:

\begin{quote}
\emph{yih ām hai.} — \textquotedblleft{}This is a mango.\textquotedblright{} (in your hand)
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{voh ām hai.} — \textquotedblleft{}That is a mango.\textquotedblright{} (on the tree)
\end{quote}

And then it does a second job that English splits across four words. The thing over there does not have to be a thing:

\begin{quote}
\emph{voh merī māṅ haiṅ.} — \textquotedblleft{}She is my mother.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Urdu names the person you are talking \textbf{about} with the same word it uses for the thing you are pointing \textbf{at}. Notice the copula in that sentence: \emph{haiṅ}, not \emph{hai}, because a mother is spoken of with respect, exactly as you already do when you address someone as \emph{āp}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{یہ}} and \textbf{\ur{وہ}} did not arrive separately. They come down together from the Old Indo-Aryan demonstratives Sanskrit wrote as \emph{iyam} — the near one — and \emph{asau} — the far one. Urdu inherited a \textbf{pair}, and it still runs the pair the way it inherited it: everything Urdu points at gets sorted into near or far first, and only then into what it actually is.

English does the same sorting with \textbf{this} and \textbf{that}, and once did it with a third, \textbf{yon}, now almost gone. But English uses separate words for the people it talks about — \emph{he}, \emph{she}, \emph{they}. Urdu keeps the far pointer doing both jobs, which is fewer words to learn and one more reason context does the work.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{voh} — that; and point at something across the room
  \item \emph{yih ām hai}, then \emph{voh ām hai}, pointing differently each time
  \item \emph{voh merī māṅ haiṅ} — and say why the copula is \emph{haiṅ}
  \item the three pointing and person words you now own — \textbf{maiṅ, yih, voh}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which is nearer, \textbf{\ur{یہ}} or \textbf{\ur{وہ}}? (\textbf{\ur{یہ}}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}that is a mango.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{voh ām hai.}) Why \emph{haiṅ} when you speak about your mother? (\textbf{Respect} — the same reason you say \emph{āp}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D9\%88\%DB\%81}{Wiktionary: \ur{وہ}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[āp kā nām kyā hai?]{The opening exchange, read off the page}

\label{lesson:UR-C18-review-aap}



\begin{quote}
Write \ur{آپ}. The wave on the alif, then the boat with three dots under it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
Here is the exchange you learned in your first hour of Urdu. Every letter in it is now one your own hand can make. Read each line from the right, naming its words, then say it:

\begin{quote}
\ur{سلام}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\ur{آپ} \ur{کا} \ur{نام} \ur{کیا} \ur{ہے؟}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\ur{میرا} \ur{نام} ... \ur{ہے۔}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\ur{آپ} \ur{کیسے} \ur{ہیں؟}
\end{quote}

\emph{salām} — \emph{āp kā nām kyā hai?} — \emph{merā nām ... hai.} — \emph{āp kaise haiṅ?}

Look at the second line. \textbf{\ur{آپ}} ends with pe wearing its full boat, and \textbf{\ur{ہے}} and \textbf{\ur{ہیں}} are the same gol he under two different endings.

Only the reply \emph{maiṅ ṭhīk hūṅ} is still out of reach, and by three shapes — one of which arrives next lesson.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Cover the page. Look, hide, write, uncover, repair.

Write these out:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \ur{آپ} \ur{کا} \ur{نام} \ur{کیا} \ur{ہے؟} — look, cover, write the whole question, uncover, repair
  \item \ur{میرا} \ur{نام} ... \ur{ہے۔} — with your own name in the gap
  \item \ur{آپ} \ur{کیسے} \ur{ہیں؟} — and check both endings against the model
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn — by ear}
Page shut. Run the whole meeting aloud with an imagined stranger, then a friend.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{salām} — \emph{āp kā nām kyā hai?} — and answer as yourself
  \item \emph{āp kaise haiṅ?} to a man, then \emph{āp kaisī haiṅ?} to a woman
  \item \emph{yih ām hai}, then \emph{voh ām hai}, and point differently
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read the question aloud from the page. (\textbf{\ur{آپ} \ur{کا} \ur{نام} \ur{کیا} \ur{ہے؟}}) Which reply can you still not write? (\emph{\textbf{maiṅ ṭhīk hūṅ}}.) How many letters do you now have? (\textbf{Twelve}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — thirteen letters, and the meeting comes off the page}

\label{lesson:UR-C18-practice}



\begin{quote}
Write the three letters this chapter has been cashing in, and name each: \ur{آ،} \ur{پ،} \ur{و}. You learned all three in chapters seven and eight.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{Nothing new is taught here.} Read each word from the right, naming its letters first:

\begin{quote}
\ur{آم}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\ur{آسمان}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\ur{پرانا}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\ur{پانی}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\ur{آپ}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\ur{وہ}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\ur{ہوں}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\ur{کون}
\end{quote}

Then the whole meeting, whole:

\begin{quote}
\ur{سلام}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\ur{آپ} \ur{کا} \ur{نام} \ur{کیا} \ur{ہے؟}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\ur{میرا} \ur{نام} ... \ur{ہے۔}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\ur{آپ} \ur{کیسے} \ur{ہیں؟}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\ur{میں} ... \ur{ہوں۔}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\ur{نہیں،} \ur{میں} \ur{کام} \ur{کر} \ur{رہا} \ur{ہوں۔}
\end{quote}

The last line is beyond what you can say yet, and it is there on purpose: every shape in it is one you can name, even where the grammar is still ahead of you. Reading has overtaken speaking for the first time.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built this chapter}]
Three letters, and three ideas worth more than the letters:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{a mark can be shorthand for a repetition} — alif madda is two alifs collapsed into one, so it opens a word and appears nowhere else
  \item \textbf{dots outlive shapes} — pe's boat shrinks to a tooth when it joins, its three dots stay, and on a crowded page you count dots rather than hunt curves
  \item \textbf{non-joiners come in a family} — with vāʾo beside alif, the gaps inside Urdu words stop being surprises
\end{itemize}

And the chapter's real argument: \textbf{\ur{پ}} exists because Arabic has no \textbf{p} and Persian built the letter Urdu now uses. The alphabet was borrowed and then altered, and the alterations are visible if you count dots.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Page covered. Hear the word — or say it to yourself from the romanization — then write it in Urdu with no model in front of you, and only then compare.

Write these out:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item hear \emph{āp}, write \textbf{\ur{آپ}}, compare
  \item hear \emph{hūṅ}, write \textbf{\ur{ہوں}}, compare
  \item hear \emph{voh ām hai}, write it whole, compare and repair
  \item hear \emph{āp kā nām kyā hai?}, write it whole, compare and repair
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many letters can you now write? (\textbf{Thirteen}.) Which of \textbf{\ur{آم}}/\emph{mango} and \textbf{\ur{آسمان}}/\emph{hammer} is a real cousin pair? (\textbf{\ur{آسمان}} and \emph{hammer}.) Why does \textbf{\ur{پ}} carry three dots? (\textbf{Persian invented it} for a sound Arabic lacks.)
\end{tcolorbox}
